title: Breast Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Breast cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: Metastasis is common to the bone, lung, and brain. Look for evidence on imaging.
Remember that lymph nodes on the opposite (i.e. contralateral) side or in the neck are distant metastases (M+).
If M+, Stage IV can be assigned and there is no need to look for further information.
Look for tumour extension to breast skin (epidermis).
Regional lymph nodes are (all on the same side of the tumour): Intramammary, Ipsilateral axillary, Infraclavicular, Internal mammary, Supraclavicular nodes.
Size of the tumour is a critical aspect, and a tumour that measures 2 cm or less is very limited (Stage I).
If two malignant tumours are present in the same breast, use the largest one to stage.

title: Cervical Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Cervical cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; FIGO, International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; N/A, not applicable; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: Distant metastasis is common to the bone, lung, and brain. Look for evidence on imaging.
Invasion of the tumour into the bladder, the rectum, or beyond the pelvis is very advanced (A2) and is considered Stage IV.
Regional lymph nodes are (pelvic nodes): Paracervical, Parametrial, Hypogastric (internal iliac, obturator), Common iliac, External iliac, Presacral, Lateral sacral nodes.
When looking for information on regional nodes, also look for mention of para-aortic nodes.
Look for tumour extension to the lower third of the vagina, or to the wall of the pelvis, or hydronephrosis due to obstruction of the ureter.
Most cervical cancers are staged using the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) system, for which the codes for stage (I–IV) are the same as those of the TNM system.

title: Oesophageal Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Oesophageal cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: The classification is for squamous cell carcinomas and aims to divide cancers into those that are operable (localized) and those that are not.
Metastasis is most common to the liver, lung, distant lymph nodes, and bone.
Regional lymph nodes are those nodes in the oesophageal drainage area: Coeliac axis nodes, Paraoesophageal nodes in the neck (but not the supraclavicular nodes).
Look for tumour extension to adjacent organs (pleura, pericardium, azygos vein, diaphragm, peritoneum, aorta, vertebral body, trachea) → the tumour is advanced (T4).

title: Colorectal Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Colorectal cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: Metastasis is most common to the liver. This may be clinically documented in operative reports or on imaging.
Regional nodes are site-specific for each segment of the colon or rectum and are named accordingly (epicolic, mesenteric, paracolic, ileocolic, rectal).

Tumour deposits (satellites) are cancer nodules that are separate from the primary tumour, located in the same area as the regional lymph nodes (pericolic or perirectal tissues). It is assumed that they represent lymph node involvement and are coded as R+.
Look for tumour extension through the wall of the colon or rectum into the subserosa or beyond, rather than tumour size.

title: Liver Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Liver cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: The classification is for hepatocellular carcinomas and aims to divide cancers into those that are operable (localized or limited) and those that are not.
Metastatic disease includes ascites with evidence of malignant spread to the peritoneum.
Regional lymph nodes are: Hilar, Hepatic (along the proper hepatic artery), Periportal (along the portal vein), Inferior phrenic, Caval nodes.

Look for tumour extension into a major branch of the portal or hepatic vein, direct invasion of adjacent organs other than the gallbladder (including the diaphragm), or perforation of the visceral peritoneum; the tumour is advanced (T4).
If it involves only the liver (or the liver and the gallbladder), look for the number of tumours in the liver; if none measures more than 5 cm, it is limited; otherwise it is advanced (T3).

title: Ovarian Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Ovarian cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis. Includes malignant cells in ascites or peritoneal washings.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: The classification applies to malignant ovarian neoplasms of both epithelial and stromal origin, including those of borderline malignancy or low malignant potential. It is also used for carcinomas of the fallopian tubes.

Metastases in the abdomen must involve the parenchyma (internal part) of organs (especially the liver) and not just the outer capsule. Spread to extra-abdominal organs and lymph nodes outside the abdominal cavity (including inguinal lymph nodes) is distant metastasis. Spread of the tumour to the peritoneum is local spread.
Regional lymph nodes are: Paracervical, Parametrial, Hypogastric (internal iliac, obturator), Common iliac, External iliac, Presacral, Lateral sacral, Para-aortic nodes.

Look for tumour extension beyond the pelvis (including to the peritoneum) or to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes; the tumour is advanced. If it is still within the pelvis, even with spread to the bowel and/or peritoneum, the tumour is localized.
Most ovarian cancers are staged using the FIGO system, which does not consider regional lymph node involvement, but the codes for stage (I–IV) are otherwise identical to those of the TNM system.

title: Prostate Cancer Essential TNM
figure_description: Prostate cancer Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; M, distant metastasis; R, regional lymph nodes; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: Distant metastasis is most common to the bone. Look for evidence of this on imaging.
Remember that distant nodes beyond the pelvis are M+. These include: Aortic (para-aortic, lumbar), Common iliac, Inguinal (femoral and deep), Supraclavicular, Cervical, Scalene, Retroperitoneal.
Regional nodes are those of the true pelvis, i.e. pelvic nodes below the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries: Obturator, Periprostatic, Perivesical, Pelvic, Iliac, Sacral, Hypogastric.
Look for tumour extension beyond the prostate capsule; if it is confined to the prostate, the tumour is localized (L).

title: Lymphoma Essential TNM
figure_description: Lymphoma Essential TNM flow chart. A, advanced extension; L, localized extension; TNM, Tumour, Node, Metastasis. *Common extralymphatic organs include bone marrow, brain, liver, lung, and gastrointestinal tract. **Nodal group = lymphatic structures including lymph nodes, Waldeyer ring, spleen, appendix, thymus, and Peyer patches.
attribution: IARC Essential TNM Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 IGO)
key_points: The TNM and Essential TNM classification for lymphomas applies to both Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Remember that lymphomas can have lymphatic and extralymphatic disease.
Lymphatic disease involves lymph nodes as well as other lymphatic structures such as the Waldeyer ring (tonsils), spleen, appendix, thymus, and Peyer patches (lymphoid tissue in the small intestine).
Staging of lymphomas may include an initial report of a bone marrow biopsy.

Look for documentation of disseminated (multifocal) involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs (such as bone marrow, brain, liver, lung, and gastrointestinal tract). This is advanced disease (Stage IV).
Look for involvement of lymphatic nodes on both sides of the diaphragm, which may be accompanied by involvement of the spleen. This is advanced disease (Stage III).
